name: Governance and compliance
description: Policies, approvals, audit trails, GDPR/HIPAA/PCI/FERPA, risk scoring.

cards.subject: A policy
says: states what must happen and why in the organisation's own rules
is approved by management and applies to everyone in scope
sets the mandatory rule without spelling out each click or keystroke
cards.use: need a binding statement of what the organisation requires
not: describes optional tips staff may ignore

cards.subject: A standard
says: sets a specific measurable requirement that supports a policy
turns a broad rule into a checkable minimum such as a required password length
is mandatory but narrower than the policy it supports
cards.use: need a concrete minimum that an auditor can test
not: is a non-binding suggestion

cards.subject: A procedure
says: lists the steps a person follows to carry out a task
says who does what and in which order
helps a new joiner repeat a task the same way every time
cards.use: need a new starter to perform a recurring task consistently
not: sets the high-level principle behind the rule

cards.subject: A guideline
says: offers advice on good practice that people may adapt
explains how to meet a policy when several approaches would work
is recommended rather than enforced
cards.use: want to share good practice without making it compulsory
not: is automatically enforced by an audit

cards.subject: A control
says: is the mechanism that makes a policy rule hard to skip
can be a technical block, a review step or a manual check
turns a written rule into something that can be tested
cards.use: need to show that a rule is actually followed rather than only written
not: is the written rule itself

cards.subject: Preventive control
says: stops a bad event from happening in the first place
includes a required approval before a change goes live
blocks the action instead of reporting it afterwards
cards.use: want the mistake to be impossible rather than merely noticed
not: finds a problem only after it has happened

cards.subject: Detective control
says: finds a problem after it has happened
includes a regular review of access logs for unusual activity
raises an alert so someone can respond
cards.use: cannot block the action but need to spot misuse quickly
not: prevents the event from occurring at all

cards.subject: Corrective control
says: limits damage and restores normal service after an incident
includes restoring from a backup or reversing a wrong entry
acts once something has already gone wrong
cards.use: need to fix and recover after a failure has been found
not: is the same as a policy approval

cards.subject: Compensating control
says: stands in for a required control that cannot be applied
adds extra monitoring or review to cover a known gap
needs to reduce the risk about as much as the missing control would
cards.use: cannot meet a requirement as written and must cover the gap another way
not: removes the need to document the gap

cards.subject: A policy exception
says: is a formal, time-limited permission to depart from a policy
records who accepted the risk and when it will be reviewed
is approved by the owner who is accountable for the risk
cards.use: have a genuine reason that a rule cannot be met for now
not: is granted verbally and never written down

cards.subject: Risk appetite
says: states how much risk the organisation is willing to accept to reach its goals
sets the boundary that individual risk decisions are judged against
is set by senior leadership rather than by each team
cards.use: need to decide whether a risk is acceptable or must be reduced
not: is the number of risks currently on the register

cards.subject: Segregation of duties
says: means the person who prepares something is not the person who approves it
stops one mistake or one bad actor pushing a change all the way through alone
is a classic control in finance and software release
cards.use: want one person unable to complete a risky process end to end
not: gives every employee the same access so work can be shared

cards.subject: The four-eyes principle
says: requires a second person to check an action before it takes effect
applies to a sensitive action even when the first person is trusted
reduces the chance of an unnoticed error
cards.use: need a second pair of eyes before a sensitive action
not: lets the author approve their own work after a break

cards.subject: A versioned approval
says: applies to one exact version of the thing approved
becomes invalid if the content changes afterwards
records who approved, what version and when
cards.use: need an approval to stay tied to exactly what the approver saw
not: covers every later edit of the same document

cards.subject: A frozen review fingerprint
says: is a value computed from the underlying numbers when GG Money freezes a brand review
stops matching if the ledger moves before approval
lets the system detect that the figures changed after the review was frozen
cards.use: want GG Money to notice that figures moved after a review was frozen
not: encrypts the review so only the approver can read it

cards.subject: A stale approval
says: is what a GG Money review becomes when its fingerprint no longer matches the ledger
has to be put up again for approval
shows that the approved numbers are not the current numbers
cards.use: find that the ledger changed between freezing and approving a review
not: keeps its approval and only shows a warning banner

cards.subject: An advisory automated check
says: gathers evidence quickly and advises but never signs off
in GG Money flags issues for a person to consider
cannot take accountability for the decision
cards.use: want a machine to collect evidence but a person to decide
not: approves a review automatically when all checks are green

cards.subject: Human sign-off
says: puts a named person's accountability on the decision
is the only kind of approval GG Money accepts for a brand review
adds judgement about things an automatic check cannot see
cards.use: need a decision that someone is answerable for
not: can be given by an AI agent calling the API

cards.subject: An evidence record
says: keeps proof that a control was carried out, such as who approved and when
lets a reviewer check a decision long afterwards
is stored with the decision rather than in someone's memory
cards.use: need to prove later that a control really happened
not: is a verbal assurance given at the time

cards.subject: Delegation of authority
says: gives another named person the right to approve while the owner is away
has a defined limit and an end date
is recorded so the later decision can be traced to the delegate
cards.use: are unavailable and an approval cannot wait
not: lets the delegate pass the approval on to anyone

cards.subject: An approval matrix
says: lists which decisions need which level of approval
often scales approvers with the size or risk of the decision
stops people guessing who must sign off
cards.use: are unsure who has to approve a given type of request
not: is a list of staff holidays

cards.subject: Rubber-stamping
says: is approving without really reading what is being approved
turns an approval step into paperwork without protection
is more likely when approvers are flooded with low-risk requests
cards.use: notice approvers clicking approve within seconds on every request
not: is a recognised good practice for speed

cards.subject: An audit trail
says: records who did what, to which record, when and with what result
lets you reconstruct events after the fact
must be hard to alter to be trusted
cards.use: need to answer who changed a record and when
not: records only the final state of the data

cards.subject: Immutability
says: means a record cannot be edited or deleted once written
preserves the original entry even when it was wrong
is what GG Money applies to posted journals
cards.use: want records that nobody can quietly rewrite
not: lets an administrator overwrite old entries

cards.subject: A reversal entry
says: corrects a posted GG Money journal by adding an opposite entry
leaves both the error and the fix visible
is the accepted way to fix a mistake in an immutable ledger
cards.use: find a mistake in a posted journal
not: deletes the original journal and re-enters it

cards.subject: A retention period
says: is how long a kind of record must be kept
depends on the legal and business obligations that apply
ends with archiving or disposal according to policy
cards.use: need to decide how long to keep a type of record
not: is the same for every record type everywhere

cards.subject: A retention class
says: groups records of one kind so each kind has its own keep period in the Moksy audit service
gives authentication events one year and payments seven years in the configuration
falls back to a two-year default when none matches
cards.use: need records of different kinds kept for different lengths
not: is a user permission level

cards.subject: The default class
says: is where every Moksy audit record landed when callers never passed a class
made the per-class retention policy govern nothing in that period
is no longer the fate of records whose action name has a known prefix
cards.use: find that all audit records share one keep period
not: only applies to payment records

cards.subject: Class derived from action prefix
says: works out a Moksy audit record's class from the start of its action name
maps prefixes such as auth or payments to their classes
is overridden when the caller passes an explicit class
cards.use: want records classified without every caller remembering to say so
not: ignores an explicit class passed by the caller

cards.subject: A retention sweep
says: archives Moksy audit records that are past their retention
never deletes them
should also report what it did not do
cards.use: need to move old audit records out of the live store safely
not: purges expired records permanently on a timer

cards.subject: A purge
says: permanently destroys records past retention
is a deliberate super-admin decision in the Moksy audit service
should not happen on an automatic timer because destroying history is a legal choice
cards.use: must permanently remove records for a legitimate reason
not: is the routine housekeeping done by the sweep

cards.subject: Archiving
says: moves records to cheaper or slower storage while keeping them retrievable
keeps old evidence available for audits
differs from deletion because the record still exists
cards.use: want old records out of daily use but still available
not: permanently removes the data

cards.subject: A legal hold
says: suspends deletion of records that may be needed in a dispute or investigation
overrides the normal retention schedule until it is lifted
is issued by legal or compliance rather than by the data owner
cards.use: learn that records may be needed for a legal matter
not: is lifted automatically at the end of the retention period

cards.subject: An email log
says: in GG Money records who sent what, when and what the provider said
deliberately omits the message body
avoids keeping a second copy of sensitive content like a payslip email
cards.use: need proof an email went out without copying its content
not: stores the full text of every email for debugging

cards.subject: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
says: requires a valid legal basis for using personal data
expects people to be told clearly how their data is used
rules out handling personal data in ways that would be unfair to the person
cards.use: need to justify why you may handle someone's personal data at all
not: lets you use data in secret if it is useful

cards.subject: Purpose limitation
says: says data collected for one stated purpose is not reused for an incompatible one
means the purpose is decided and stated before collection
stops a customer list gathered for billing being quietly used for unrelated marketing
cards.use: are tempted to reuse data for something new
not: allows any later use if the data is already held

cards.subject: Data minimisation
says: means collecting only what you need for the stated purpose
applies to how much is collected, not just how long it is kept
is why GG Money's email log omits the message body
cards.use: are designing a form or log and deciding which fields to keep
not: says to collect everything in case it is useful later

cards.subject: Accuracy
says: requires personal data to be correct and kept up to date
means wrong data must be corrected or erased without delay
protects people from decisions based on faulty records
cards.use: discover that a stored detail about a person is out of date
not: means data can be left as first entered

cards.subject: Storage limitation
says: says personal data is kept no longer than needed for its purpose
is applied through retention schedules and disposal
differs from minimisation because it is about time, not quantity
cards.use: ask how long personal data may stay in a system
not: lets data be kept forever once it is archived

cards.subject: Integrity and confidentiality
says: requires personal data to be protected against loss, damage and unauthorised access
is met with measures such as access control, encryption and backups
is the security principle of data protection law
cards.use: are choosing technical safeguards for personal data
not: only applies to data stored on paper

cards.subject: Accountability
says: makes the organisation responsible for showing it complies
is met by keeping records, policies and evidence
means saying you comply is not enough without proof
cards.use: are asked to prove compliance to a regulator
not: is satisfied by a verbal promise to follow the rules

cards.subject: A lawful basis
says: is the legal ground that permits processing personal data
can be consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests
should be identified before processing begins
cards.use: need to state why personal data may be processed
not: is always the person's consent

cards.subject: Consent
says: must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous when it is the lawful basis
can be withdrawn as easily as it was given
is not valid when it comes from a pre-ticked box
cards.use: rely on a person's agreement as the reason to process data
not: is valid when it is bundled into terms nobody reads

cards.subject: The right of access
says: lets a person get a copy of the personal data held about them
also entitles the person to know why and how it is used
is exercised through a subject access request
cards.use: receive a request from a person asking what data you hold on them
not: lets a person read other people's data in the same file

cards.subject: The right to rectification
says: lets a person have inaccurate personal data corrected
also covers completing data that is incomplete
connects to the accuracy principle
cards.use: have been told that a stored detail about a person is wrong
not: lets a person delete the whole record

cards.subject: The right to erasure
says: lets a person ask for their personal data to be deleted in certain cases
is not absolute and can be refused where a legal obligation requires keeping the data
is often called the right to be forgotten
cards.use: get a request from a person to delete their data
not: always overrides every legal record-keeping duty

cards.subject: The right to restriction
says: lets a person ask that data be stored but not otherwise used
applies for example while the accuracy of the data is being checked
pauses processing without deleting
cards.use: must stop using data while a dispute about it is resolved
not: means the data must be destroyed at once

cards.subject: The right to data portability
says: lets a person receive their data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format
can let the person have it passed to another provider
applies to data the person supplied under consent or contract
cards.use: get a request from a person to move their data to a competitor
not: covers every note the organisation wrote about them

cards.subject: The right to object
says: lets a person object to processing based on legitimate interests
is absolute for direct marketing
forces the organisation to stop unless it shows compelling grounds
cards.use: are told by a person to stop using their data for marketing
not: can be refused for direct marketing if the data is useful

cards.subject: The right on automated decisions
says: protects people from decisions made solely by automated processing that significantly affect them
lets a person ask for human intervention and contest the decision
matters when AI scores or ranks people
cards.use: let an AI system alone decide something important about a person
not: only applies to decisions made on paper

cards.subject: Breach notification
says: requires regulators to be told of a personal data breach within a short deadline where there is risk to people
can require the affected people to be told when the risk is high
relies on the organisation detecting and escalating quickly
cards.use: discover that personal data was exposed
not: can wait until the next annual audit

cards.subject: GDPR
says: is the European Union data protection regulation
applies to organisations handling personal data of people in the EU wherever the organisation is based
rests on principles such as minimisation, purpose limitation and accountability
cards.use: handle personal data about people in Europe
not: is a United States health-information law

cards.subject: PCI DSS
says: is an industry standard for organisations that handle payment card data
is safest met by avoiding touching card numbers at all
is set by the card brands, not by a government
cards.use: take card payments in your system
not: is a law about student records

cards.subject: HIPAA
says: is a United States law that protects health information
applies to covered organisations and their suppliers
includes rules about how health records are accessed and disclosed
cards.use: you work with health records of people in the United States
not: is the European data protection regulation

cards.subject: FERPA
says: is a United States law that protects student education records
gives students or parents rights to inspect and correct those records
restricts schools from disclosing records without consent
cards.use: you handle school student records in the United States
not: governs payment card security

cards.subject: SOC 2
says: is an independent auditor's report on controls against trust services criteria
covers areas such as security, availability and confidentiality
is requested by customers as assurance about a service provider
cards.use: are asked by a customer for assurance about your service controls
not: is a law passed by a government

cards.subject: ISO 27001
says: is an international standard for an information security management system
can be certified by an accredited external body
is organised around risk assessment and continual improvement
cards.use: want a recognised certification of your security management
not: is a United States privacy statute

cards.subject: CCPA
says: is a California privacy law
gives residents rights to know about and delete the personal information collected about them
lets residents opt out of the sale of their personal information
cards.use: you serve consumers in California
not: applies only inside the European Union

cards.subject: A data processing agreement
says: is a contract that binds a supplier to handle personal data only on the organisation's instructions
sets security and sub-supplier terms for the processor
is required when a supplier processes personal data on your behalf
cards.use: bring in a supplier who will process personal data for you
not: is optional when the supplier is trusted

cards.subject: Data classification
says: sorts information into levels such as public, internal, confidential and restricted
decides how strongly each kind of data is protected
gives staff a simple way to know how careful to be
cards.use: need to know how carefully a piece of information must be handled
not: is a list of who may log in

cards.subject: Personal data
says: is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person
includes names, email addresses and online identifiers
is protected by data protection law
cards.use: are deciding whether a field falls under data protection rules
not: covers only information that is marked confidential

cards.subject: Special category data
says: is personal data such as health, biometrics or religious belief that needs extra protection
normally needs an additional condition before it can be processed
carries higher risk of harm if exposed
cards.use: design a feature that records health or biometric details
not: is treated exactly like ordinary contact details

cards.subject: Pseudonymisation
says: replaces direct identifiers with a code while a key is kept separately
still counts as personal data because it can be reversed with the key
reduces risk without removing it
cards.use: want to work with data while hiding identities but keep the ability to re-link
not: makes the data permanently anonymous

cards.subject: Anonymised data
says: cannot be linked back to a person by any reasonable means
falls outside data protection law when truly anonymous
is hard to achieve because combining datasets can re-identify people
cards.use: want to share statistics with no way to identify anyone
not: is the same as removing the name column

cards.subject: Masking
says: hides part of a value so only a safe portion is visible
shows for example only the last digits of a number
is what Moksy's scrub rules do to email addresses and phone numbers in text
cards.use: need to show or pass on data without exposing the full value
not: encrypts the whole database file

cards.subject: Encryption at rest
says: protects stored data so a stolen disk or backup is unreadable
does not protect data from a user who is already logged in with access
depends on keeping the keys separate and safe
cards.use: worry about a lost laptop or stolen backup
not: protects data while it moves across the network

cards.subject: Encryption in transit
says: protects data as it moves between systems or across a network
is provided for web traffic by TLS
stops eavesdropping on the connection
cards.use: send sensitive data over the internet
not: protects data sitting on a disk

cards.subject: Data mapping
says: records what personal data is held, where it flows and who receives it
underpins the records of processing an organisation must keep
reveals forgotten copies such as a debugging table
cards.use: need to find every place personal data lives
not: lists only the databases that IT owns

cards.subject: A data protection impact assessment
says: assesses risks to people before a high-risk use of personal data begins
is expected for large-scale or new technology uses such as profiling
identifies measures to reduce those risks
cards.use: plan a new system that profiles people at scale
not: is done once a year for every system

cards.subject: Privacy by design
says: builds data protection into a system from the start
favours defaults that collect and expose the least data
is cheaper than bolting controls on later
cards.use: are starting to design a new feature that handles personal data
not: adds privacy notices after launch

cards.subject: A sandbox redirect address
says: in a GG Money sandbox install is the address that receives email instead of real recipients
means nothing is sent unless one is set
stops a test from emailing a real employee
cards.use: test email features without risking messages to real people
not: sends real payslips to staff during tests

cards.subject: Tokenisation of card data
says: replaces a card number with a token that is useless outside the payment system
shrinks the amount of card data an organisation holds
helps reduce the scope of payment card compliance
cards.use: want to take repeat card payments without storing card numbers
not: stores the full card number in an encrypted column

cards.subject: A risk score
says: combines likelihood and impact into one comparable figure
is commonly worked out by multiplying the two
lets a rare severe event rank alongside a frequent minor one
cards.use: need to compare very different worries
not: measures how many controls have been written

cards.subject: Likelihood
says: is how probable it is that a risk event will happen
is one of the two inputs to a simple risk score
needs evidence such as incident history to be estimated well
cards.use: are rating how probable a problem is
not: is the damage if the event happens

cards.subject: Impact
says: is how bad the consequences are if the risk event happens
is the second input to a simple risk score
is made visible in GG Money's compliance calendar by writing what goes wrong if a task is missed
cards.use: are rating the consequences of a problem
not: is how often the event occurs

cards.subject: A risk register
says: lists identified risks with their scores, owners and treatments
is reviewed so it stays current
gives leaders one place to see the main exposures
cards.use: need one place that tracks known risks
not: lists only risks that have already happened

cards.subject: A risk owner
says: is the named person accountable for managing one risk
decides with the organisation how it will be treated
is a person, not a team mailbox
cards.use: need someone answerable for a specific risk
not: is the person who first spotted it

cards.subject: Inherent risk
says: is the level of risk before any controls are applied
shows how exposed you would be with no protection
is compared with residual risk to see what controls achieve
cards.use: want to judge how risky an activity is with no controls
not: is the risk left after controls work

cards.subject: Residual risk
says: is the risk that remains after controls are applied
must be accepted or further reduced
rises if a control is untested or fails
cards.use: ask what exposure is left after existing controls
not: is the risk before controls

cards.subject: Risk mitigation
says: reduces the likelihood or impact of a risk
is done through controls and changes
is chosen when the risk is too high but the activity is worth keeping
cards.use: decide to add controls to bring a risk down
not: means accepting the risk as it is

cards.subject: Risk acceptance
says: knowingly lives with a risk because it falls within appetite or the cost to reduce it is too high
should be recorded and approved by the risk owner
is a decision, not a default for ignored risks
cards.use: decide a small risk is not worth the cost of reducing
not: happens automatically when nobody addresses a risk

cards.subject: Risk transfer
says: shifts some of the financial impact to another party such as an insurer or supplier
does not remove the original responsibility to manage the risk
is common for losses that are rare but expensive
cards.use: buy insurance against a rare costly event
not: makes the risk disappear

cards.subject: Risk avoidance
says: stops the activity that creates the risk
removes the exposure entirely at the cost of the benefit
is chosen when a risk is above appetite and cannot be reduced enough
cards.use: decide to stop doing something because the risk is too high
not: adds monitoring without changing the activity

cards.subject: A compliance calendar
says: in GG Money lists each recurring task with its frequency, sign-off owner, source rule and consequence of missing it
states that dates are reminders, not advice
marks some dates as needing confirmation because facts like a first accounting period sit outside the app
cards.use: need to track recurring obligations and who signs them off
not: is legal advice that guarantees deadlines are right

cards.subject: Key risk indicator
says: is a measure that warns a risk is rising before an incident
tracks something like overdue reviews or failed backups
is watched against thresholds that trigger action
cards.use: want an early signal that exposure is growing
not: counts incidents after the year ends

cards.subject: Least privilege
says: gives people only the access they need to do their job
limits the damage if an account is misused or compromised
is reviewed as roles change
cards.use: are deciding how much access a new person should get
not: gives everyone admin rights to avoid delays

cards.subject: Role-based access control
says: grants permissions to roles rather than to individuals
gives a person the access of the role they hold
makes access easier to review and to change when someone moves
cards.use: want permissions to follow job roles
not: assigns each permission by hand to individual people

cards.subject: Need to know
says: limits sensitive information to people who require it for their task
applies even to senior people who hold a high clearance
is narrower than being in the right role
cards.use: someone asks for sensitive data out of curiosity
not: gives access to anyone at the same grade

cards.subject: An access review
says: checks periodically that each person's access is still appropriate
is signed off by the owner of the system or data
catches access that built up as people changed roles
cards.use: want to catch access that is no longer needed
not: is done only when someone leaves

cards.subject: Joiner-mover-leaver process
says: adjusts access when people start, change role or leave
removes old permissions when someone moves rather than only adding new ones
revokes access promptly on departure
cards.use: see a colleague move to a different team
not: only grants access to new starters

cards.subject: Offboarding
says: removes a leaver's access and recovers their equipment
happens on or before their last day
closes accounts so none are left active unused
cards.use: learn that a person is leaving the company
not: waits until the next access review

cards.subject: Multi-factor authentication
says: requires two or more different kinds of proof of identity
still protects an account when a password is stolen
combines something you know with something you have or are
cards.use: want an account to survive a leaked password
not: is satisfied by entering two passwords

cards.subject: Single sign-on
says: lets one login give access to many services
centralises where accounts are created and removed
makes offboarding more reliable
cards.use: want one place to manage who can use many tools
not: stores each service's password in the browser of each user

cards.subject: Privileged access
says: gives powerful rights such as administering systems
needs stronger approval, logging and review than ordinary access
is granted for the time it is needed rather than permanently
cards.use: need elevated rights to administer a system
not: is shared freely so the team can cover for each other

cards.subject: Break-glass access
says: is emergency access used only when normal routes fail
is heavily logged and reviewed afterwards
should be rare and time-limited
cards.use: normal approval is down and a critical outage needs urgent fixing
not: is a normal way to skip approvals when busy

cards.subject: A shared account
says: is one login used by several people
breaks the audit trail because actions cannot be tied to one person
should be avoided in favour of named accounts
cards.use: find a login that the whole team uses
not: improves accountability because everyone knows the password

cards.subject: A service account
says: is an account used by software rather than a person
should have only the permissions its job needs
has its credentials rotated and owned by a named person
cards.use: need an application to connect to another system
not: is a good place to store a team's shared password

cards.subject: A change request
says: records what will change, why, and who is responsible
is raised before the change is made
gives approvers something specific to review
cards.use: need to make a change to a live system
not: is filed after the change is live to tidy the records

cards.subject: Change control
says: is the process that decides which changes go ahead and how
reduces unplanned outages from untracked changes
keeps a record of each change and its approval
cards.use: want changes to a system to be controlled and traceable
not: slows every change down with no benefit

cards.subject: Peer review
says: has a colleague examine a change before it is accepted
catches mistakes the author cannot see
applies the four-eyes principle to code and documents
cards.use: have finished a change and want it checked
not: is performed by the author themselves

cards.subject: A rollback plan
says: says how to return to the previous working state if a change fails
is agreed before the change is made
is tested rather than assumed
cards.use: worry that a deployment might break production
not: is written only after the change has failed

cards.subject: Testing in staging
says: checks a change in a copy of production before it goes live
finds problems without affecting real users
is only reliable if staging resembles production
cards.use: want to try a change without risk to real users
not: means testing directly on production

cards.subject: Separation of environments
says: keeps development, testing and production apart
prevents test data from reaching real customers
means real personal data is not copied into development without protection
cards.use: are asked why developers should not use production data
not: lets developers edit production directly for speed

cards.subject: An emergency change
says: is a fast-tracked fix for an urgent live problem
still needs to be recorded and approved after the fact
is reviewed afterwards to see whether the shortcut was justified
cards.use: need a fix for a live outage right now
not: skips all records because there is no time

cards.subject: A change freeze
says: pauses non-urgent changes during a sensitive period
protects stability around events such as a year-end close
lets only emergency changes through
cards.use: want to avoid new risk during a critical period
not: blocks all changes including emergency fixes

cards.subject: Traceability
says: links a change back to its request, approval and test
lets an auditor follow a change from the reason to the result
depends on references such as ticket numbers in commit messages
cards.use: are asked to show why a particular change was made
not: is the same as keeping the code in a backup

cards.subject: A post-implementation review
says: checks after a change whether it achieved its aim and what went wrong
feeds lessons into the next change
compares the outcome with the plan
cards.use: want to learn from a change that has just gone live
not: is done before the change is approved

cards.subject: A code of conduct
says: sets out the behaviour the organisation expects from everyone
gives a shared reference for ethical decisions
applies to every person regardless of seniority
cards.use: are unsure whether a behaviour is acceptable here
not: applies only to new starters

cards.subject: A conflict of interest
says: arises when a personal interest could influence a work decision
should be declared even if you think it will not affect you
is managed by disclosure and by stepping back from the decision
cards.use: are asked to choose a supplier run by a relative
not: is harmless as long as nobody finds out

cards.subject: A gift
says: needs checking against the gifts policy when a supplier offers it
is declared when it could look like an attempt to influence a decision
may need to be refused or returned if it is of more than modest value
cards.use: receive a valuable present from a supplier before a contract decision
not: can be accepted privately if it is a surprise

cards.subject: Bribery
says: is offering or accepting something of value to improperly influence a decision
is a crime in most countries even when done through an agent
cannot be justified as a local custom
cards.use: are asked to pay a facilitation fee to speed an approval
not: is only an offence when the money is large

cards.subject: Whistleblowing
says: is reporting suspected wrongdoing through a protected channel
is protected by law in many places against retaliation
lets concerns reach someone who can act when the usual line manager is involved
cards.use: suspect serious wrongdoing and your manager may be part of it
not: is a breach of loyalty that should be avoided

cards.subject: Speaking up
says: means raising a concern early before it becomes a larger problem
is encouraged for mistakes as well as for misconduct
depends on people not being blamed for good-faith reports
cards.use: notice a mistake that could harm a customer
not: means waiting until the audit finds it

cards.subject: Confidentiality
says: means not sharing non-public information with people who should not have it
continues after you leave the organisation
covers customer, staff and company information
cards.use: hold information that is not meant to be public
not: ends on your last day

cards.subject: An acceptable use policy
says: sets out how company systems and accounts may be used
covers things such as installing software and using personal devices
is what staff agree to follow
cards.use: want to know whether you may use work equipment for something
not: is only relevant to the IT team

cards.subject: Phishing reporting
says: means passing a suspicious message to the security team
helps protect colleagues who might get the same message
is better than deleting it quietly or replying
cards.use: receive an email that asks you urgently for a password
not: is unnecessary once you have deleted the message

cards.subject: Ethics
says: asks what is right as well as what is legal
guides decisions where no rule gives a clear answer
is about judgement in the moment, not just rule-following
cards.use: face a decision that is legal but could harm someone
not: is satisfied by obeying the law and nothing more

cards.subject: Compliance
says: is following the laws, regulations and internal policies that apply
needs evidence that rules are followed, not just intention
can be met on paper while the real behaviour differs
cards.use: are asked what compliance means
not: is the same as ethics

cards.subject: Governance
says: is the system of rules, roles and decisions by which an organisation is directed and held accountable
defines who decides what and who is answerable
pairs policies with controls that can be checked
cards.use: are asked what governance means
not: is the daily work of the helpdesk

cards.subject: An AI usage policy
says: says which AI tools staff may use and for what
sets rules for what data may be entered into them
applies to everyone using AI at work
cards.use: want to know what you may put into an AI tool
not: bans staff from ever reading AI output

cards.subject: Human in the loop
says: keeps a person responsible for the decision an AI suggests
is how GG Money lets AI agents leave notes but only a person approve
lets someone catch wrong or unfair output before it takes effect
cards.use: see an AI system propose an action with real consequences
not: lets the AI act unattended once it passes a test

cards.subject: Shadow AI
says: is use of AI tools that the organisation has not approved
can send company or customer data to an unvetted provider
is reduced by offering approved tools that meet real needs
cards.use: find colleagues pasting customer data into an unapproved chatbot
not: is fine as long as the output is correct

cards.subject: An AI scrub rule
says: in Moksy's AI policy service masks email addresses and phone numbers before text travels onwards
removes personal identifiers from a prompt before it leaves
applies data minimisation to AI traffic
cards.use: want personal details removed from text sent to a model
not: encrypts the AI provider's response

cards.subject: Hallucination risk
says: is the chance that an AI states false things confidently
means important AI output must be checked against a source
is why AI output should not be accepted without review in regulated work
cards.use: plan to rely on AI output in a document that others will act on
not: only occurs when the user prompts badly

cards.subject: Bias in AI
says: is a systematic unfair skew in an AI system's results
can come from unrepresentative training data
needs testing for different groups of people to find
cards.use: worry that an AI screening tool treats groups differently
not: disappears when the model is large enough

cards.subject: A secret in a prompt
says: is a credential or confidential value pasted into an AI tool
may be stored or seen by a third party
should be kept out of prompts and replaced with placeholders
cards.use: are about to paste an access key into an AI assistant to get help
not: is safe because the chat is private

cards.subject: AI record keeping
says: logs AI events so use can be reviewed
is covered in Moksy's retention classes with its own keep period
supports accountability for what the AI did
cards.use: need to show later what an AI system did and when
not: is unnecessary because the model remembers

cards.subject: Prompt injection
says: is text in input that tries to make an AI follow the attacker's instructions
can come from a web page or document the AI reads
is why AI agents should be given the least permission they need
cards.use: let an AI agent read untrusted content while it has access to tools
not: is prevented by telling the model to ignore it

cards.subject: AI transparency
says: means telling people when they are dealing with AI or AI-assisted output
helps users decide how far to trust it
supports the right to contest automated decisions
cards.use: customers might not realise a reply was machine-written
not: is satisfied by a hidden note in the source code

cards.subject: An internal audit
says: is a check on controls carried out by the organisation's own independent function
reports findings to senior management
tests whether controls work as described
cards.use: want an independent look at controls without bringing in an outside firm
not: is done by the team that owns the control

cards.subject: An external audit
says: is carried out by an independent outside firm
gives stakeholders confidence in the organisation's figures or controls
is separate from the organisation's internal checks
cards.use: need independent assurance for a customer or regulator
not: is carried out by the organisation's own staff

cards.subject: An audit finding
says: is a recorded gap between what was found and what should be in place
is rated by severity
needs an owner and a date for the fix
cards.use: hear an auditor report that a control did not work
not: is a verbal remark that does not need tracking

cards.subject: Corrective action
says: is the fix agreed for an audit finding or incident
has an owner and a due date
addresses the root cause, not only the symptom
cards.use: need to fix a finding and stop it recurring
not: is closed as soon as the symptom disappears

cards.subject: Audit sampling
says: tests a subset of items instead of all of them
lets an auditor reach a conclusion about the whole population
works only if the sample is chosen without bias
cards.use: cannot test every record but must draw a conclusion
not: means testing only the records the owner picks

cards.subject: The three lines model
says: separates operational management, risk and compliance oversight, and independent audit
puts the day-to-day ownership of risk with the first line
has internal audit as the independent third line
cards.use: want to see who owns, oversees and independently checks risk
not: makes the compliance team own all risk

cards.subject: Records management
says: controls how records are created, kept and disposed of
uses a retention schedule to say how long each type is kept
helps find the right record when it is needed
cards.use: need to decide how records are kept and disposed of
not: means keeping everything forever

cards.subject: Document control
says: makes sure people use the current approved version of a document
keeps version history and approval status
retires old versions so they are not used by mistake
cards.use: worry that staff are following an outdated procedure
not: lets anyone edit the live policy

cards.subject: An incident report
says: describes what happened, the impact and the actions taken
should be raised as soon as an incident is noticed
feeds lessons back into controls
cards.use: notice a security or data incident
not: is held back until the cause is certain

cards.subject: Compliance calendar testing
says: checks that scheduled obligation dates are right for different circumstances
treats the calendar as a system that can be wrong
is motivated by an October 2026 GG Money stress run that proposed some statutory dates could be a day or two late for certain year ends
cards.use: want to be sure a deadline list will not mislead people
not: is unnecessary once the calendar is published

cards.subject: Surfacing by risk
says: shows high-severity items first instead of only the oldest
avoids a capped list of routine tasks hiding statutory deadlines
is the lesson of a backlog of daily housekeeping tasks in GG Money's calendar
cards.use: find that low-severity noise is burying important deadlines
not: sorts every task strictly by age

qa.q: Which of these is an example of segregation of duties?
qa.right: The person who prepares a payment is not the person who approves it
wrong: The manager prepares and approves every payment to save time
Everyone in the team shares one login for payments
Payments are approved by whoever is free first, including the preparer
qa.why: Separating preparation from approval means no single person can complete a risky action alone.

qa.q: What should you do first if you receive an email asking you urgently to confirm your password?
qa.right: Report it to the security team and do not reply
wrong: Reply asking whether it is genuine
Click the link to check if it works, then close it
Delete it quietly and tell nobody
qa.why: Reporting protects colleagues who may receive the same message.

qa.q: What is the main purpose of an audit trail?
qa.right: To show who did what, to which record and when
wrong: To speed up the system
To remove the need for passwords
To store a copy of every file in the company
qa.why: A trail lets events be reconstructed after the fact.

qa.q: Which statement best describes data minimisation?
qa.right: Collect only the personal data you need for the stated purpose
wrong: Collect as much as possible in case it is useful later
Keep data forever but encrypt it
Collect data first and decide on a purpose afterwards
qa.why: Minimisation limits how much is collected, which limits exposure.

qa.q: A policy and a control are different. Which sentence is correct?
qa.right: A policy states the rule, and a control is the mechanism that makes it hard to skip
wrong: A policy and a control are two names for the same document
A control is a written rule and a policy is a technical block
A policy is checked by auditors but a control never is
qa.why: Governance pairs the rule with something that can be tested.

qa.q: Which of these is personal data?
qa.right: An email address that identifies a customer
wrong: A company's public product price list
The total number of orders last year across all customers
A software version number
qa.why: Information relating to an identifiable person is personal data.

qa.q: Your teammate asks to approve their own expense claim because the approver is away. What is the right response?
qa.right: Ask for a documented delegation to another approver
wrong: Let them approve it and mention it later
Approve it yourself without telling anyone
Skip approval because the claim is small
qa.why: A delegate keeps the preparer and approver separate and leaves a record.

qa.q: In GG Money, why do automatic compliance checks never sign off a review?
qa.right: Sign-off needs a named person who takes responsibility
wrong: Automatic checks are always wrong
Sign-off is only for senior staff
The checks run too slowly to finish
qa.why: Machines gather evidence; a human takes accountability.

qa.q: How does GG Money correct a mistake in a posted journal?
qa.right: By posting a reversal so both the error and the fix stay visible
wrong: By editing the journal in place
By deleting the journal and posting a new one
By hiding it from reports
qa.why: Immutable ledgers are corrected with additional entries.

qa.q: A customer asks what personal data you hold about them. Which right are they using?
qa.right: The right of access
wrong: The right to erasure
The right to portability only
The right to restriction
qa.why: Access is the right to a copy of the data and the reasons for processing.

qa.q: Which framework is an industry standard for organisations that handle payment card data?
qa.right: PCI DSS
wrong: HIPAA
FERPA
GDPR
qa.why: PCI DSS is set by the card brands for card data.

qa.q: What does least privilege mean for a new starter?
qa.right: They get only the access their job needs
wrong: They get the same access as their manager
They get no access until their first review
They get admin rights for the first month
qa.why: Limited access limits the damage from misuse or compromise.

qa.q: Which email data does GG Money deliberately NOT store in its email log?
qa.right: The message body
wrong: The time the email was sent
Who the email was sent to
What the email provider said
qa.why: A payslip body holds someone's salary, and a second copy is a liability.

qa.q: You find a mistake in a colleague's document just after it was published. What is the best habit?
qa.right: Tell them promptly and follow the correction process
wrong: Wait for the audit to find it
Quietly edit the live version without a record
Ignore it because it is not your document
qa.why: Speaking up early keeps small errors small, and a record keeps the correction traceable.

qa.q: Under GDPR-style law, what does storage limitation require?
qa.right: Keeping personal data no longer than needed for its purpose
wrong: Storing all data in one country
Encrypting all data
Keeping data for exactly seven years
qa.why: It is about time, while minimisation is about quantity.

qa.q: A GG Money brand review was frozen and a ledger entry changed before approval. What happens?
qa.right: The fingerprint no longer matches, so the review goes stale and has to be put up again
wrong: The approver is told but the review stays approved
The ledger change is rolled back automatically
The review is approved automatically using the new figures
qa.why: An approval belongs to one exact version of the figures.

qa.q: What is the best reason a frozen review carries a fingerprint of its numbers?
qa.right: It lets a change to the underlying figures be detected before approval counts
wrong: It encrypts the numbers
It makes the page load faster
It counts how many times the review was opened
qa.why: The fingerprint ties the approval to the exact numbers shown.

qa.q: According to the Moksy audit service configuration, which pairing of retention class and keep period is correct?
qa.right: Payments seven years
wrong: Authentication events seven years
Payments one year
AI events seven years
qa.why: The configured values are authentication one year, payments seven years, AI events two years and a two-year default.

qa.q: How long does the Moksy audit service keep authentication events, according to its configuration?
qa.right: One year
wrong: Seven years
Two years
Forever
qa.why: Authentication events are configured at one year; the values are configuration, not legal advice.

qa.q: What did Moksy audit callers' failure to pass a class cause?
qa.right: Every record fell into the default class, so per-class policy governed nothing
wrong: Every record was deleted immediately
Every record was kept for seven years
Every record was rejected
qa.why: Deriving the class from the action prefix fixed it, and an explicit class still wins.

qa.q: How does the Moksy audit service now work out a record's class when none is passed?
qa.right: From the action name prefix such as auth or payments
wrong: From the time of day it was written
From the size of the record
From the user's job title
qa.why: An explicit class passed by the caller still takes priority.

qa.q: What does the Moksy retention sweep do to records past their retention?
qa.right: Archives them without deleting them
wrong: Deletes them permanently
Hands them to the user who created them
Moves them to the default class
qa.why: Purging remains a deliberate super-admin decision.

qa.q: A sandbox install of GG Money has no redirect address set. What happens when a test tries to send email?
qa.right: Nothing is sent
wrong: It is sent to real employees
It is sent to the developer's personal email
It is sent to the audit service
qa.why: A sandbox sends nothing unless a redirect address is set, so tests cannot email real employees.

qa.q: What does the Moksy AI policy service scrub rule do?
qa.right: Masks email addresses and phone numbers in text before it travels onwards
wrong: Encrypts the model's reply
Blocks all AI requests after midnight
Deletes AI logs after one day
qa.why: It applies data minimisation to AI traffic.

qa.q: What does a GG Money compliance calendar entry state about each task?
qa.right: How often it recurs, who signs it off, the rule it comes from and what goes wrong if missed
wrong: Only the due date
Only the person who created it
The legal penalty in each country
qa.why: Writing the consequence makes the impact visible so tasks can be ranked.

qa.q: What does the GG Money compliance calendar say about its dates?
qa.right: They are reminders, not advice
wrong: They are legal advice that is always correct
They are final and cannot be changed
They apply only to the first accounting period
qa.why: Some dates are marked as needing confirmation.

qa.q: What is the difference between a preventive and a detective control?
qa.right: Preventive stops the event happening, detective finds it afterwards
wrong: Preventive finds it afterwards, detective stops it
Both work only after the event
They are the same control used by different teams
qa.why: A required approval is preventive; a log review is detective.

qa.q: Which is a correct use of a risk score?
qa.right: Compare a rare severe event with a frequent minor one
wrong: Prove that a control works
Replace the need for an audit
Decide who is to blame for an incident
qa.why: Likelihood multiplied by impact gives a comparable figure.

qa.q: Which authentication setup is multi-factor?
qa.right: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
wrong: Two different passwords
A password plus a security question
The same password typed twice
qa.why: Different kinds of factor are needed: know, have, are.

qa.q: What does a change request give an approver?
qa.right: Something specific to review: what changes, why and who is responsible
wrong: A reason to skip testing
Permission for any later change
A list of staff holidays
qa.why: It is raised before the change is made.

qa.q: Which describes consent as a GDPR lawful basis?
qa.right: It must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous
wrong: It can be assumed from silence
It is valid inside long terms nobody reads
It cannot be withdrawn once given
qa.why: Pre-ticked boxes and silence do not count.

qa.q: A supplier offers you an expensive gift while you are choosing between suppliers. What should you do?
qa.right: Decline it or declare it under the gifts policy
wrong: Accept it if nobody saw
Accept it and choose that supplier fairly anyway
Keep it and tell nobody until the contract is signed
qa.why: A gift at that moment could look like an attempt to influence your decision.

qa.q: A new feature will profile customers at large scale. What should happen before launch?
qa.right: A data protection impact assessment
wrong: Nothing, as risks appear after launch
Only a privacy notice after launch
A retention sweep
qa.why: High-risk processing should be assessed before it starts.

qa.q: Why is deleting the first copy of a record not enough to meet an erasure request?
qa.right: Other copies such as logs and backups may also hold the data
wrong: Erasure only applies to paper
Copies are never personal data
Erasure requests are always refused
qa.why: Data mapping helps find forgotten copies.

qa.q: Your team lead says an approval step is slowing delivery and proposes letting developers approve their own low-risk changes. What is the best response?
qa.right: Keep separation but make the step lighter for low-risk changes, for example through an approval matrix
wrong: Agree, as low risk means no control is needed
Add three more approvers to every change
Move approvals to after release for all changes
qa.why: Scale the control to the risk instead of removing separation.

qa.q: A team finds that all their audit records are kept for the two-year default. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: Callers are not passing a class and nothing derives it
wrong: Authentication events are too numerous
The sweep deletes everything
The default is a legal minimum
qa.why: This mirrors the past Moksy gap, which prefix-derived classes fixed.

qa.q: A sweep job runs nightly and its log shows no errors. What more should you want from it?
qa.right: A report of what it skipped or did not do
wrong: A longer log with more timestamps
Permission to purge anything it skipped
A manual approval for each record
qa.why: A sweep should also report what it did not do, so silent gaps are visible.

qa.q: An engineer wants to copy production customer data into a development database to debug. What is the best response?
qa.right: Use masked or synthetic data instead
wrong: Allow it if they are trusted
Allow it for a week then ask them to delete it
Copy it but rename the database
qa.why: Real personal data should not move into development unprotected.

qa.q: A GG Money-style review is approved, then the underlying numbers move. What should the process do with the approval?
qa.right: Treat it as no longer valid and require a new approval
wrong: Keep it because the approver was trusted
Edit the approval date to today
Delete the review
qa.why: The approval applies to the exact version approved.

qa.q: An AI agent calls an internal API and offers to approve a brand review that its checks cleared. What is the right design?
qa.right: Let the agent leave a note and require a named person to approve
wrong: Let the agent approve if all checks pass
Let the agent approve if a manager is on holiday
Let the agent approve and notify later
qa.why: Automation advises; a person is accountable.

qa.q: A deadline list is capped at 50 items and a backlog of daily housekeeping tasks fills it. What risk does this create?
qa.right: Statutory deadlines could be hidden below the cap
wrong: The list loads too slowly
The tasks will be double counted
Auditors will ignore the daily tasks
qa.why: Surfacing by risk avoids noise burying severity.

qa.q: A control has never failed in five years. What can you safely conclude?
qa.right: Nothing yet, because it may never have been tested
wrong: The control is perfect
The risk is zero
The control can be removed
qa.why: A control with no failures may simply never have been tested.

qa.q: A person asks you to stop using their data for direct marketing. What must you do?
qa.right: Stop, because the right to object is absolute for direct marketing
wrong: Refuse if the data is useful
Continue until they put it in writing twice
Stop only after 12 months
qa.why: The objection to direct marketing cannot be refused.

qa.q: A vendor will process customer personal data for you. What do you need in place?
qa.right: A data processing agreement
wrong: Only a verbal promise
A copy of their marketing brochure
Nothing if they are well known
qa.why: The contract binds them to process only on your instructions.

qa.q: Two administrators share one admin login to cover each other. What is the main governance problem?
qa.right: Actions cannot be tied to one person, breaking the audit trail
wrong: It costs more in licences
The login will expire sooner
It stops multi-factor authentication being useful
qa.why: Named accounts keep accountability.

qa.q: A team cannot meet a required control for three months. What is the best approach?
qa.right: Raise a time-limited policy exception with a compensating control
wrong: Ignore the requirement until it is audited
Mark the control as passed
Disable the check
qa.why: The exception records who accepted the risk and when it will be reviewed.

qa.q: After a test run, a compliance calendar shows a statutory date one day late for a certain year end. What does that tell you?
qa.right: The calendar is a system that needs testing like any other
wrong: Dates should be ignored
The auditors are wrong
The year end is unusual so no fix is needed
qa.why: An October 2026 stress run proposed exactly this kind of issue; nothing was fixed at that time.

qa.q: A legal dispute is expected. The retention period for some records ends next week. What should happen?
qa.right: Apply a legal hold so the records are not deleted
wrong: Let the sweep delete them to reduce exposure
Archive them to a personal drive
Edit them to remove sensitive content
qa.why: A legal hold overrides the normal schedule.

qa.q: An AI agent that reads web pages has permission to send email. What is the key risk?
qa.right: Prompt injection could make it send email on an attacker's instruction
wrong: The web pages will be too large
It will charge more for tokens
It will be unable to read images
qa.why: Give agents only the permission they need.

qa.q: An approver approves 200 requests in ten minutes. What is the likely governance problem?
qa.right: Rubber-stamping that gives no real protection
wrong: The approver is working efficiently
The requests must be low risk
The approval matrix has too few levels
qa.why: Approvals that are not read provide no control.

qa.q: An auditor samples 25 records out of 5,000 and the owner picks which 25. What is the weakness?
qa.right: The sample may be biased so conclusions about the whole may be wrong
wrong: The sample is too large
Owners cannot see their own records
Sampling is not allowed in audits
qa.why: A sample must be chosen without bias to support a conclusion.

qa.q: Several ranked-low risks sit together on the register. What second-order effect should you check?
qa.right: Whether they share a cause and could fail together
wrong: Whether they are alphabetically ordered
Whether they have the same author
Whether they can be merged into one score
qa.why: Correlated risks can combine into a larger one than any score shows.

qa.q: A company relies on automated decisions to reject loan applicants. Which governance step best protects people?
qa.right: Offer human review and a way to contest the decision
wrong: Hide that automation is used
Make rejections irreversible
Remove the audit log to save cost
qa.why: People have a right to contest solely automated significant decisions.

qa.q: After an emergency change in production, what is the best next step?
qa.right: Record and review it afterwards to see if the shortcut was justified
wrong: Delete the ticket to avoid blame
Treat all future changes the same way
Assume it was fine because it worked
qa.why: Emergency changes still need a record and review.

qa.q: A supplier's SOC 2 report is two years old. What is the best judgement?
qa.right: Ask for a current report or other evidence, because the old one says little about today
wrong: Accept it, as SOC 2 never expires
Reject the supplier automatically
Ask the supplier to certify verbally
qa.why: Assurance reports describe a period, and controls change.

qa.q: The retention sweep job fails silently for months. Which control type would have caught this?
qa.right: A detective control such as a monitored report of sweep outcomes
wrong: A rollback plan
A policy exception
Stronger passwords
qa.why: Monitoring that checks the sweep ran and what it did not do finds silent failure.
